title: Iraqi Arabic grammar
about: Only what Iraqi Arabic does differently from Modern Standard Arabic, in 16 short lessons: how it sounds, the words for I, what, where and why, aku and māku, how to say “not”, “want”, “-ing”, “will” and “still”, the verb endings, numbers and “if”. Everything else works as in Standard Arabic, so the Arabic grammar course comes first. Every example is Arabic as people in Baghdad say it, with vowel marks, گ for the Iraqi g and چ for ch, and a reading in Latin letters; you can tap it to hear it.

lessons.title: Sound like Baghdad
lessons.summary: Say {{گَال}} “he said” and {{چِبِير}} “big” the way people in Baghdad do: the few sound changes that make Standard Arabic sound Iraqi.
lessons.topic: Sounds: {{ق}} said g ({{گ}}), {{ك}} said ch in some words ({{چ}}), ē and ō, helping vowels

goal.tr: She said: the house is big.

dialog.tr: How are you? What's the news?
I'm fine too. Where are you going?

blocks.p: This course builds on Standard Arabic (MSA). It teaches only what is **different** in the Arabic spoken in Iraq, in the style of Baghdad: the variety heard most on Iraqi TV and understood all over the country. Everything not mentioned here works as in MSA: the letters, the roots, most words, {{عِنْدِي}} “I have”, and the order of words.

blocks.means: the everyday spoken Arabic of one region (here: Iraq, Baghdad style), as opposed to Modern Standard Arabic, the Arabic of books and the news.

blocks.p: **{{ق}} is mostly said g**, and this course writes it {{گ}}: {{گَال|gāl}} “he said”, {{سُوگ|sūg}} “market”, {{گْرِيب|grīb}} “near”, {{گَلُب|galub}} “heart”. Religious and formal words keep the standard q: {{الْقُرْآن|il-qurʾān}}, {{قَانُون|qānūn}} “law”. A few words say k instead: {{وَكِت|wakit}} “time” (MSA {{وَقْت}}).

**{{ك}} is said ch in some words**, written {{چ}}, mostly next to an i or e sound: {{چَان|chān}} “was”, {{چِبِير|chibīr}} “big”, {{چَلِب|chalib}} “dog”, {{چَم|cham}} “how many”, and the ending “your” to a woman: {{بَيْتِچ|bētich}} “your house”. Many words keep k: {{كْتَاب|ktāb}} “book”, {{كُلّ|kull}} “every”. Learn each word with its sound.

**{{ث}} and {{ذ}} stay.** Unlike Cairo or Damascus, Baghdadis keep the “th” sounds of MSA: {{ثْلَاثَة|thlātha}} “three”, {{هَذَا|hādha}} “this”. **{{ض}} is said like {{ظ}}**, a heavy “dh”: {{أَبْيَض|abyaḍh}} “white”. **ay and aw become ē and ō**: {{بَيْت|bēt}} “house”, {{يَوْم|yōm}} “day”. And **two consonants at the end of a word get a helping vowel**: {{گَلُب|galub}}, {{چَلِب|chalib}}, {{وَكِت|wakit}}.

blocks.tip: **Spelling.** Iraqis write their dialect with ordinary Arabic letters, and online they often write g as {{ك}} or {{ق}} and ch as {{ج}} ({{كَال}}, {{هِيج}}). This course uses {{گ}} and {{چ}}, as Iraqi dictionaries do, so you always know the sound; the Latin reading under each example shows how it is said. Your card voice can't say {{گ}} and {{چ}}, so when you tap an example it says those letters the Standard way (q, k); the recordings of the Iraqi basics course say them right.

mistakes.why: In everyday words {{ق}} is said g.

practice.q: How does someone from Baghdad say {{قَال}} “he said”?
practice.why: {{ق}} is said g, and the final vowel goes: gāl, written {{گَال}}.

practice.q: Which sound do Baghdadis **keep**, unlike Cairo and Damascus?
practice.why: Baghdadis keep {{ث}} and {{ذ}}: thlātha, hādha. {{قَلْب}} is galub, {{كَبِير}} is chibīr.

practice.q: Say “She said: the house is big”, the Baghdad way.
Your turn: say three words with the Baghdad g or ch, for example {{گَال}}, {{سُوگ}}, {{چِبِير}}.

lessons.title: Drop the endings
lessons.summary: Say {{بِالْبَيْت}} “at home” and {{يَوْمَيْن}} “two days” without MSA's endings, and keep the -ūn of {{يِلْعَبُون}} “they play”.
lessons.topic: No case endings; the dual only on nouns (-ēn); “in” {{بِـ}}; present -ūn and -īn kept

goal.tr: The two boys are playing outside.

dialog.tr: Let them come, the food is ready.

blocks.p: **No case endings.** MSA nouns end in -u, -a, -i or -un to show their role ({{فِي الْبَيْتِ}}); Iraqi drops them all: {{بِالْبَيْت|bil-bēt}} “at home”. “In, at” is usually {{بِـ}} joined to the next word: {{بِبَغْدَاد|bi-baghdād}} “in Baghdad”, {{بِالسُّوگ|bis-sūg}} “at the market”.

blocks.means: the short vowel at the end of an MSA noun (-u, -a, -i, -un) that shows its role in the sentence. Spoken Arabic leaves it out.

blocks.p: **The dual is only for nouns**, with the ending -ēn: {{يَوْمَيْن|yōmēn}} “two days”, {{سَاعْتَيْن|sāʿtēn}} “two hours”. Everything that goes with the two is plural: {{بَيْتَيْن چْبَار|bētēn chbār}} “two big houses”, {{هُمَّه|humma}} “they”, {{يِلْعَبُون|yilʿabūn}} “they play”.

**The present keeps -ūn and -īn**, as MSA does (Cairo and Damascus drop them): {{يِكِتْبُون|yikitbūn}} “they write”, {{تِكِتْبُون|tikitbūn}} “you all write”, {{تِكِتْبِين|tikitbīn}} “you (a woman) write”.

ex.tr: I stayed two days in Baghdad.
Where do you work? (to a woman)

blocks.tip: Words that end in {{ة}} are said -a: {{سَاعَة|sāʿa}} “hour”, {{سَيَّارَة|sayyāra}} “car”. Before an ending it is -at or -t: {{سَيَّارْتِي|sayyārti}} “my car”.

mistakes.why: That's MSA. In Baghdad: no case ending, and “in, at” is usually {{بِـ}}.
Only the noun takes the dual; the adjective is plural.

practice.why: -ēn is the dual ending of nouns: {{يَوْم}} “day”, {{يَوْمَيْن}} “two days”.

practice.q: A friend asks about your trip.

lines.tr: How long did you stay in Baghdad?

lines.why: The dual ends in -ēn: {{يَوْمَيْن}}. -ān is MSA.

practice.q: Your turn: say how long you stayed somewhere, with a dual: {{يَوْمَيْن}}, {{سَاعْتَيْن}}…

answers.tr: I stayed two days in Basra.

lessons.title: Say “I”, “we”, “you” and “my, your”
lessons.summary: Say {{آنِي}} “I”, {{إِحْنَا}} “we” and {{بَيْتِچ}} “your house” to a woman: the Iraqi pronouns and endings.

dialog.t: لَا، هَذَا بَيْت أَهْلِي. إِحْنَا سَاكْنِين بِالْكَرَّادَة.
dialog.r: la, hādha bēt ahli. iḥna sāknīn bil-karrāda.
dialog.tr: No, it's my parents' house. We live in Karrada.
And are your parents here too?

blocks.p: **The pronouns.** Most look like MSA, said the Iraqi way. Three are new: {{آنِي|āni}} “I”, {{إِحْنَا|iḥna}} “we” and {{هُمَّه|humma}} “they”.
Many Baghdadis also keep words for women only: {{إِنْتِن|intin}} “you (women)” and {{هِنَّه|hinna}} “they (women)”. You will hear them; {{إِنْتُو}} and {{هُمَّه}} are always understood.

blocks.means: a piece added to the end of a noun that says whose it is: -i “my”, -ak “your”. The same endings on a verb or a word like “with” mean “me, you, him”.

blocks.p: **The endings** are MSA's, with two Iraqi ones: **-a “his”** (written {{ـَه}}): {{بَيْتَه|bēta}} “his house”; and **-ich “your” to a woman**: {{بَيْتِچ|bētich}}. In full: {{بَيْتِي|bēti}}, {{بَيْتَك|bētak}}, {{بَيْتِچ|bētich}}, {{بَيْتَه|bēta}}, {{بَيْتْهَا|bētha}}, {{بَيْتْنَا|bētna}}, {{بَيْتْكُم|bētkum}}, {{بَيْتْهُم|bēthum}}. They go on verbs and little words too: {{شَافْنِي|shāfni}} “he saw me”, {{وِيَّاچ|wiyyāch}} “with you (a woman)”.

blocks.tip: {{وِيَّا|wiyya}} “with” is very Iraqi: {{وِيَّاي|wiyyāy}} “with me”, {{وِيَّاك|wiyyāk}} “with you”, {{وِيَّا أَهْلَه|wiyya ahla}} “with his family”.

practice.tr: Is this your house? (to a woman)

practice.q: Your turn: say who you are and where you're from, and ask a woman where she's from.

answers.tr: I'm Sarah, from London. And you?

lessons.title: Ask what, who, where, why and how

goal.tr: What's your name? Where do you live?

blocks.p: The question word comes first, as in MSA, but the words are Iraqi:

blocks.means: a word that asks for a piece of information: what, who, where, why, how, when.

blocks.p: **{{شْـ}} is “what” joined to the next word**: {{شْتْرِيد؟|shtrīd?}} “what do you want?”, {{شْبِيك؟|shbīk?}} “what's wrong with you?”, {{شَكُو؟|shaku?}} “what's up?”. To ask a price, say {{بَيْش؟|bēsh?}} “for how much?”.

blocks.tip: {{شْلَوْن}} “how” is also how Iraqis greet: {{شْلَوْنَك؟|shlōnak?}} to a man, {{شْلَوْنِچ؟|shlōnich?}} to a woman, {{شْلَوْنْكُم؟|shlōnkum?}} to several. The answer: {{زَيْن|zēn}} or {{الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰه|il-ḥamdu lillāh}}.

mistakes.why: “What” is {{شِنُو}}, or {{شْـ}} joined to the verb.

practice.q: You buy tea at a stall.

lines.why: He asks what you want: say it, then ask the price with {{بَيْش}}.

practice.q: Your turn: ask a new colleague three questions: their name, where they're from, where they live.

answers.t: شِنُو اسْمَك؟ مِنَيْن إِنْتَ؟ وَيْن سَاكِن؟
answers.r: shinu ismak? minēn inta? wēn sākin?
answers.tr: What's your name? Where are you from? Where do you live?

lessons.title: Point: this, that, like this
lessons.summary: Point with {{هَذَا}}, {{هَاي}} and {{هَذَوْل}} “this, these”, {{ذَاك}} and {{ذِيچ}} “that”, and say {{هِيچ}} “like this”.

goal.tr: This is my daughter, and this is my son.

dialog.tr: This one is two thousand, and that one a thousand.
That one's better. I want that one.

blocks.p: “This” changes with the word it points at: {{هَذَا|hādha}} for a masculine word, {{هَاي|hāy}} for a feminine one, {{هَذَوْل|hadhōl}} for several. “That”: {{ذَاك|dhāk}}, {{ذِيچ|dhīch}}, {{ذَوْلَاك|dhōlāk}}.

blocks.means: a pointing word: this, that, these, those.

blocks.p: Before a noun you can use the short {{هَالـ|hal-}} “this, these” for all of them: {{هَالْبَيْت|hal-bēt}} “this house”, {{هَالسَّيَّارَة|has-sayyāra}} “this car”. And “here, there” are {{هْنَا|hnā}} and {{هْنَاك|hnāk}}.

ex.tr: Why are you talking like that?

blocks.tip: {{هِيچ}} “like this, so” is everywhere: {{هِيچ أَحْسَن|hīch aḥsan}} “it's better like this”, {{مُو هِيچ؟|mū hīch?}} “isn't that so?”. Online it is often written {{هِيج}}.

practice.q: Which word points at a feminine word, “this”?

practice.tr: Why are you talking like that?

lines.why: {{بَيْش}} asks the price; {{ذِيچ}} points at a feminine word far off.
{{هِيچ هْوَايَة}} “that much!”, a start to bargaining.

practice.q: Your turn: point at two things near you and say what they are, with {{هَذَا}} and {{هَاي}}.

answers.tr: This is my phone, and this is my car.

lessons.title: Say what there is: aku and māku
lessons.summary: Say {{أَكُو}} “there is” and {{مَاكُو}} “there isn't”, and ask {{شَكُو مَاكُو؟}} “what's up?”.

goal.tr: Is there a restaurant here? No, there isn't.

dialog.tr: There's a party tomorrow, are you coming?

blocks.p: **{{أَكُو|aku}} is “there is, there are”**, and **{{مَاكُو|māku}} “there isn't, there aren't”**. They never change: {{أَكُو نَاس|aku nās}} “there are people”, {{مَاكُو مُشْكِلَة|māku mushkila}} “there's no problem”. In a question, the voice goes up: {{أَكُو مَاي؟|aku māy?}} “is there any water?”.

blocks.means: a word that says something exists or is there: “there is”, “there are”.

blocks.p: **Past and future:** put {{چَان|chān}} “was” or {{رَاح يْكُون|rāḥ ykūn}} “will be” in front: {{چَان أَكُو زَحْمَة|chān aku zaḥma}} “there was a traffic jam”, {{مَا چَان أَكُو|ma chān aku}} “there wasn't”.
**{{شَكُو مَاكُو؟|shaku māku?}}**, literally “what is there and what isn't?”, is the Iraqi “what's up?, what's new?”. The answer: {{مَاكُو شِي|māku shī}} “nothing much”.

ex.tr: There were a lot of people.
Do you have any money on you?

blocks.tip: {{مَاكُو}} also answers “no” to a question with {{أَكُو}}: {{أَكُو خُبُز؟ مَاكُو.|aku khubuz? māku.}} “Is there bread? There isn't.”

practice.q: A friend asks {{شَكُو مَاكُو؟}}. They want to know…

lines.tr: No, there's none since the morning.

lines.why: Ask why: {{لَيْش}}, and {{شْبِيهَا؟}} “what's wrong with it?”.

practice.tr: There were a lot of people.

practice.q: Your turn: say two things there are and one thing there isn't where you live.

answers.t: أَكُو سُوگ وِمَطْعَم، بَسّ مَاكُو مَسْبَح.
answers.r: aku sūg w-maṭʿam, bass māku masbaḥ.
answers.tr: There's a market and a restaurant, but there's no pool.

lessons.title: Say what isn't so
lessons.summary: Say “not” with {{مَا}} before a verb and {{مُو}} before everything else, “don't!” with {{لَا}}, and {{مَحَّد}} “nobody”.
lessons.topic: {{مَا}} + verb, {{مُو}} + noun or adjective, {{لَا}} + command, {{مَحَّد}}, {{وَلَا شِي}}

goal.t: مَا أَعْرُف، آنِي مُو مِن هْنَا.
goal.r: ma aʿruf, āni mū min hnā.
goal.tr: I don't know, I'm not from here.

dialog.tr: Do you know where the hospital is?

dialog.t: لَا، مَا أَعْرُف. آنِي مُو مِن هَالْمَنْطِگَة.
dialog.r: la, ma aʿruf. āni mū min hal-manṭiga.
dialog.tr: No, I don't know. I'm not from this area.

blocks.p: **{{مَا|ma}} before a verb**, in any tense: {{مَا أَعْرُف|ma aʿruf}} “I don't know”, {{مَا جَا|ma ja}} “he didn't come”, {{مَا رَاح يْرُوح|ma rāḥ yrūḥ}} “he won't go”.

**{{مُو|mū}} before everything else**: a noun, an adjective, a place or a word like “here”: {{مُو زَيْن|mū zēn}} “not good”, {{مُو هْنَا|mū hnā}} “not here”, {{هَذَا مُو بَيْتِي|hādha mū bēti}} “this isn't my house”. At the end of a sentence, {{مُو؟}} asks “isn't it?”. One exception: “have” ({{عِنْدِي}}, {{وِيَّاي}}) takes {{مَا}}: {{مَا عِنْدِي وَكِت|ma ʿindi wakit}} “I don't have time”.

blocks.means: making a sentence say “not”: “I know” becomes “I don't know”.

blocks.p: **{{لَا|la}} before a command** says “don't”: {{لَا تْرُوح|la trūḥ}} “don't go”, {{لَا تِحْچِي|la tiḥchi}} “don't talk”. And “nobody” is {{مَحَّد|maḥḥad}}, “nothing” {{وَلَا شِي|wala shī}}.

ex.tr: I don't like tea without sugar.

blocks.tip: {{مَا يْخَالِف|ma ykhālif}}, literally “it doesn't go against (anything)”, is the Iraqi “no problem, it's OK”.

mistakes.why: {{مَا}} goes with verbs; {{مُو}} with everything else.

practice.tr: I don't know where his house is.

practice.q: Someone at the door asks for your brother.
Your turn: say one thing you don't like and one thing that isn't true about you.

answers.t: مَا أَحِبّ الْبَرْد، وِآنِي مُو تَعْبَان.
answers.r: ma aḥibb il-bard, w-āni mū taʿbān.
answers.tr: I don't like the cold, and I'm not tired.

lessons.title: Count, pay and tell your age
lessons.summary: Count from {{وَاحِد}} to {{عِشْرِين}} the Iraqi way, say prices in dinars and ask {{شْگَدّ عُمْرَك؟}} “how old are you?”.
lessons.topic: Numbers 1-20, 11-19 in -ʿash and -ṭaʿash, {{مِيَّة}}, {{أَلِف}}, counting things, prices

blocks.p: The numbers are MSA's, said the Iraqi way: {{وَاحِد|wāḥid}}, {{ثْنَيْن|thnēn}}, {{ثْلَاثَة|thlātha}}, {{أَرْبَعَة|arbaʿa}}, {{خَمْسَة|khamsa}}, {{سِتَّة|sitta}}, {{سَبْعَة|sabʿa}}, {{ثْمَانْيَة|thmānya}}, {{تِسْعَة|tisʿa}}, {{عَشْرَة|ʿashra}}. **11 and 12 end in -ʿash, 13 to 19 in -ṭaʿash:**

blocks.means: the noun after a number: in “three kilos”, “kilos”.

blocks.p: **Counting things:** 3 to 10 take a short form and a plural, {{ثْلَث سَاعَات|thlath sāʿāt}} “three hours”, {{خَمِس دَگَايِگ|khamis dagāyig}} “five minutes”; 11 and up take the singular, {{خْمُسْطَعَش يَوْم|khmusṭaʿash yōm}} “fifteen days”. Two of something is the dual: {{سَاعْتَيْن|sāʿtēn}}. Prices are in dinars, usually in thousands: {{أَلِف|alif}}, {{أَلْفَيْن|alfēn}}, {{عِشْرِين أَلِف|ʿishrīn alif}}; and “thousands” after 3 to 10 is {{تَالَاف|tālāf}}.

blocks.tip: To ask a price, {{بَيْش؟|bēsh?}} or {{شْگَدّ سِعْرَه؟|shgadd siʿra?}} “how much is it?”. And {{شْگَدّ عُمْرَك؟|shgadd ʿumrak?}} “how old are you?”, answered {{عُمْرِي…|ʿumri…}} “my age is…”.

mistakes.why: 11 to 19 are one word, ending in -ʿash or -ṭaʿash.
After 11 and up, the noun stays singular.

practice.why: Three of something: the short {{ثْلَث}} and a plural.

lines.why: Ten of something: the short {{عَشِر}} and the plural.

practice.q: Your turn: say how old you are and how many rooms your home has.

answers.t: عُمْرِي ثْلَاثِين سَنَة، وِبَيْتِي بِيه أَرْبَع غُرَف.
answers.r: ʿumri thlāthīn sana, w-bēti bī arbaʿ ghuraf.
answers.tr: I'm thirty, and my house has four rooms.

lessons.title: Say what you want, can and must do
lessons.summary: Say {{أَرِيد}} “I want”, {{أَگْدَر}} “I can” and {{لَازِم}} “I must”, with the next verb straight after: no {{أَنْ}}.
lessons.topic: {{أَرِيد}}, {{رِدِت}}; {{أَگْدَر}}, {{مَا أَگْدَر}}; {{لَازِم}}; {{يِمْكِن}}; no {{أَنْ}} before the second verb

goal.tr: I want to go, but I can't.

dialog.tr: Do you want to come with us to the cinema?
I'd like to, but I have to study today.

blocks.p: **Want:** {{أَرِيد|arīd}} “I want”, {{تْرِيد|trīd}} “you want”, {{يْرِيد|yrīd}} “he wants”, {{نْرِيد|nrīd}} “we want”; “I wanted” is {{رِدِت|ridit}}. **Can:** {{أَگْدَر|agdar}} “I can”, {{تِگْدَر|tigdar}} “you can”, {{مَا أَگْدَر|ma agdar}} “I can't”. **Must:** {{لَازِم|lāzim}}, the same for everyone. **Maybe:** {{يِمْكِن|yimkin}}.

**The second verb comes straight after**, in the present, with no {{أَنْ}}: {{أَرِيد أَشْرَب|arīd ashrab}} “I want to drink”, {{تِگْدَر تِجِي؟|tigdar tiji?}} “can you come?”, {{لَازِم نْرُوح|lāzim nrūḥ}} “we must go”.

blocks.means: a verb like want, can or must that goes with a second verb: “I **can** swim”.

table: {{لَا أَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ آتِيَ|lā astaṭīʿu an ātiya}}

ex.tr: What do you want to eat?
I wanted to talk to you.

blocks.tip: {{خَوْش|khōsh}} “good, nice” goes before the noun: {{خَوْش فِكْرَة|khōsh fikra}} “a good idea”. And {{يَلَّا|yalla}} “come on, let's go” is everywhere.

mistakes.why: No {{أَنْ}}: the second verb comes straight after.
After {{لَازِم}}, the verb is in the present.

lines.tr: Can you go out with us tonight?
No problem. When are you free?

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you want to do, one you can't, and one you must do this week.

answers.t: أَرِيد أَرُوح لِلْبَصْرَة، بَسّ مَا أَگْدَر هَالْأُسْبُوع. لَازِم أَشْتُغُل.
answers.r: arīd arūḥ lil-baṣra, bass ma agdar hal-usbūʿ. lāzim ashtughul.
answers.tr: I want to go to Basra, but I can't this week. I have to work.

lessons.title: Say whose it is, and who with
lessons.summary: Say {{مَالِي}} “mine” and {{السَّيَّارَة مَالْتَك؟}} “is the car yours?”, and who you're with: {{وِيَّاي}}, {{وِيَّاك}}.

goal.t: هَذَا الْكْتَاب مَالِي، وِهَاي الْجَنْطَة مَالْتِچ.
goal.r: hādha il-ktāb māli, w-hāy ij-janṭa māltich.
goal.tr: This book is mine, and this bag is yours.

blocks.p: **{{مَال|māl}} “belonging to”** says whose a thing is, after the thing: {{الْكْتَاب مَالِي|il-ktāb māli}} “the book is mine”, {{السَّيَّارَة مَال أَبُويَه|is-sayyāra māl abūya}} “the car is my dad's”. It takes the possessive endings: {{مَالِي|māli}}, {{مَالَك|mālak}}, {{مَالِچ|mālich}}, {{مَالَه|māla}}, {{مَالْنَا|mālna}}, {{مَالْهُم|mālhum}}.

After a feminine word many people say {{مَالْتـ|mālt-}}: {{السَّيَّارَة مَالْتِي|is-sayyāra mālti}} “the car is mine”. Both are heard. {{مَال}} is handy where an MSA {{إِضَافَة}} would be long: {{الْبَاب مَال الْبَيْت|il-bāb māl il-bēt}} “the door of the house”.

blocks.means: a word that says whose something is, like English “of” or “'s”: “the book **of** Ali”, “Ali**'s** book”.

blocks.p: **Having** is {{عِنْدِي|ʿindi}}, as in MSA. **With** is {{وِيَّا|wiyya}}: {{وِيَّاي|wiyyāy}} “with me”, {{وِيَّاك|wiyyāk}}, {{وِيَّاچ|wiyyāch}}, {{وِيَّاه|wiyyā}} “with him”, {{وِيَّانَا|wiyyāna}} “with us”.

ex.tr: No, it's not mine. It's my brother's.
The phone is the work one.

blocks.tip: {{أَخُويَه|akhūya}} “my brother” and {{أَبُويَه|abūya}} “my dad” take an extra -ya in Iraqi.

practice.q: Your turn: say whose two things near you are, with {{مَال}}.

answers.tr: The phone is mine, and the car is my sister's.

lessons.title: Say what you do, and tell people what to do
lessons.summary: Say {{أَشْرَب چَاي كُلّ يَوْم}} “I drink tea every day” with the Iraqi present, and give orders: {{تَعَال}}, {{رُوح}}, {{اُگْعُد}}.
lessons.topic: The present without a prefix ({{أَكْتِب}}, {{يِكْتِب}}); commands; {{خَلّ}} “let's”

goal.t: آنِي أَشْتُغُل كُلّ يَوْم، بَسّ الْجُمْعَة أَرْتَاح.
goal.r: āni ashtughul kull yōm, bass ij-jumʿa artāḥ.
goal.tr: I work every day, but on Friday I rest.

dialog.tr: What do you do in the morning?

dialog.t: أَگْعُد سَبْعَة، أَشْرَب چَاي، وِأَرُوح لِلشُّغُل.
dialog.r: agʿud sabʿa, ashrab chāy, w-arūḥ lish-shughul.
dialog.tr: I get up at seven, drink tea and go to work.
And when do you come back?

blocks.p: **The present has no prefix in Baghdad** (Damascus and Cairo add b-): {{أَكْتِب|aktib}} “I write”, {{يِشْرَب|yishrab}} “he drinks”. The same form says what you do now and what you do every day; lesson 12 shows how to say “right now”.

blocks.means: the form of a verb that tells someone to do something: “go!”, “sit down!”.

blocks.p: **Commands** drop the {{تِـ}} of “you”: {{رُوح|rūḥ}} “go”, {{رُوحِي|rūḥi}} to a woman, {{رُوحُوا|rūḥu}} to several. Some everyday ones: {{تَعَال|taʿāl}} “come”, {{اُگْعُد|ugʿud}} “sit”, {{شُوف|shūf}} “look”, {{اِنْطِينِي|inṭīni}} “give me”. **Let's** is {{خَلّ|khall}} or {{خَلِّي|khalli}} with the “we” form: {{خَلّ نْرُوح|khall nrūḥ}} “let's go”.

blocks.tip: {{گِعَد|giʿad}} means “sit” and also “get up, wake up”: {{أَگْعُد سَبْعَة|agʿud sabʿa}} “I get up at seven”. The rest of the sentence makes it clear.

mistakes.why: Baghdad has no b- before the present.

practice.q: A colleague asks about your day.

lines.tr: When do you get up in the morning?

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you do every morning.

answers.tr: I get up, drink tea and go to work.

lessons.title: Say what you're doing right now
lessons.summary: Say {{دَا أَشْتُغُل}} or {{گَاعِد أَشْتُغُل}} “I'm working (right now)”, and ask {{شْدَا تْسَوِّي؟}} “what are you doing?”.

goal.t: هَسَّه دَا أَطْبُخ، أَتَّصِل بِيك بَعْدَيْن.
goal.tr: I'm cooking right now, I'll call you later.

blocks.p: The plain present also says what happens now, but to stress **right now, in the middle of it**, Baghdadis put **{{دَا|da}}** in front of it: {{دَا أَكْتِب|da-aktib}} “I'm writing”, {{دَا يِحْچِي|da-yiḥchi}} “he's talking”. With “what”, it's {{شْدَا|sh-da}}: {{شْدَا تْسَوِّي؟|sh-da-tsawwi?}} “what are you doing?”.

**{{گَاعِد|gāʿid}}** (literally “sitting”) does the same and agrees with the person: {{گَاعِد|gāʿid}} for a man, {{گَاعْدَة|gāʿda}} for a woman, {{گَاعْدِين|gāʿdīn}} for several: {{گَاعْدَة تْنَام|gāʿda tnām}} “she's sleeping”.

blocks.means: the form that shows an action going on at the moment: “I **am working**”.

blocks.tip: {{هَسَّه|hassa}} “now” is the Iraqi word (from {{هَذِهِ السَّاعَة}} “this hour”), and {{بَعْدَيْن|baʿdēn}} “later”.

lines.tr: Where are you? What are you doing?

practice.q: Your turn: say what you are doing right now, and what someone near you is doing.

answers.t: دَا أَدْرُس عَرَبِي، وِأُخْتِي گَاعْدَة تِتْفَرَّج عَالتَّلْفِزْيَوْن.
answers.r: da-adrus ʿarabi, w-ukhti gāʿda titfarraj ʿat-talfizyōn.
answers.tr: I'm studying Arabic, and my sister is watching TV.

lessons.title: Talk about your plans
lessons.summary: Say what will happen with {{رَاح}}: {{رَاح أَرُوح بَاچِر}} “I'll go tomorrow”, and when: {{بَاچِر}}, {{بَعْدَيْن}}, {{عُگُب}}.

goal.tr: Tomorrow we're going to go to Basra.

dialog.tr: What are you going to do in the holiday?
We're going to visit our family in Mosul.
Nice! When are you coming back?

blocks.p: **{{رَاح|rāḥ}} + the present** says what will happen: {{رَاح أَرُوح|rāḥ arūḥ}} “I'll go”, {{رَاح يِجِي|rāḥ yiji}} “he'll come”. It never changes. Quickly said it becomes {{رَحْ|raḥ}}: {{رَحْ أَجِي|raḥ aji}} “I'll come”.

blocks.means: the form of a verb for what will happen: “I **will go**”, “I'm **going to** go”.

blocks.p: **Not:** {{مَا رَاح|ma rāḥ}}: {{مَا رَاح أَجِي|ma rāḥ aji}} “I won't come”. **When:** {{بَاچِر|bāchir}} “tomorrow”, {{عُگُب بَاچِر|ʿugub bāchir}} “the day after tomorrow”, {{بَعْدَيْن|baʿdēn}} “later”, {{عُگُب|ʿugub}} “after, in”: {{عُگُب سَاعَة|ʿugub sāʿa}} “in an hour”.

ex.tr: We won't make it in time.
What are you going to eat?
After work I'm going to rest.

blocks.tip: Don't mix {{رَاح}} “will” with the verb {{رَاح}} “he went”: {{رَاح لِلسُّوگ|rāḥ lis-sūg}} “he went to the market”, {{رَاح يْرُوح لِلسُّوگ|rāḥ yrūḥ lis-sūg}} “he will go to the market”. A present verb after it means “will”.

mistakes.why: After {{رَاح}} “will”, the verb is in the present.

lines.tr: What are you going to do tomorrow?
Can you come after the afternoon?

practice.q: Your turn: say two things you're going to do this weekend.

answers.t: رَاح أَنَام زَيْن، وِبَعْدَيْن رَاح أَطْلَع وِيَّا رَبْعِي.
answers.r: rāḥ anām zēn, w-baʿdēn rāḥ aṭlaʿ wiyya rabʿi.
answers.tr: I'm going to sleep well, and then I'll go out with my friends.

lessons.title: Say what happened
lessons.summary: Tell what happened with the Iraqi past endings, {{رِحِت}} “I went”, {{گَالَوْا}} “they said”, and what used to happen: {{چَان يْرُوح}}.

goal.tr: Yesterday I went to the market and saw my friend.

dialog.t: طْلَعِت وِيَّا رَبْعِي، وِأَكَلْنَا سِمَچ مَسْگُوف.
dialog.r: ṭlaʿit wiyya rabʿi, w-akalna simach masgūf.
dialog.tr: I went out with my friends and we ate masgouf fish.
And what did they say about the restaurant?
They said it was really good.

blocks.p: **The past endings** are MSA's, said the Iraqi way. Two differ: **“I” and “you” (a man) are the same, -it**: {{كِتَبِت|kitabit}} “I wrote / you wrote”; and **“they” is -aw**: {{كِتْبَوْا|kitbaw}} “they wrote”.

blocks.means: the form of a verb for what happened: “I **went**”, “they **said**”.

blocks.p: **{{چَان|chān}} is “was”**: {{چِنِت|chinit}} “I was”, {{چَانَت|chānat}} “she was”, {{چِنَّا|chinna}} “we were”, {{چَانَوْا|chānaw}} “they were”. **{{چَان}} + the present** says what used to happen: {{چَان يْرُوح لِلْمَدْرَسَة مَشِي|chān yrūḥ lil-madrasa mashi}} “he used to walk to school”. **Not:** {{مَا}}: {{مَا شِفْتَه|ma shifta}} “I didn't see him”.

ex.tr: I didn't sleep well last night.
We used to play in the street.

blocks.tip: {{الْبَارْحَة|il-bārḥa}} “yesterday” and {{گَبُل|gabul}} “before, ago”: {{گَبُل سَنَة|gabul sana}} “a year ago”.

practice.tr: Yesterday I went to the market.
He used to walk to school.
practice.why: Used to: {{چَان}} + present. {{رَاح}} + present would be “will”.

practice.q: A friend asks about your weekend.

lines.tr: Where were you? I didn't see you.

lines.why: It's over, so the past: {{چَانَت}} “it was”. {{رَاح تْكُون}} is “it will be”.

practice.tr: I didn't sleep well last night.

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you did yesterday, and one thing you used to do as a child.

answers.t: الْبَارْحَة اشْتِغَلِت، طْبَخِت، وِشِفِت فِلِم. چِنِت أَلْعَب كُرَة هْوَايَة.
answers.r: il-bārḥa shtighalit, ṭbakhit, w-shifit filim. chinit alʿab kura hwāya.
answers.tr: Yesterday I worked, cooked and watched a film. I used to play football a lot.

lessons.title: Say “just”, “still”, “not yet” and “stopped”
lessons.summary: Say {{هَسَّه وِصَلِت}} “I've just arrived”, {{بَعَدْنِي}} “I'm still”, {{بَعَد مَا}} “not yet” and {{بَطَّل}} “stopped”.

goal.tr: I haven't eaten yet, I've just arrived.

blocks.p: **Just:** {{هَسَّه|hassa}} “now” before a past verb: {{هَسَّه وِصَلِت|hassa wṣalit}} “I've just arrived”.

**Still:** {{بَعَد|baʿad}} with an ending says who: {{بَعَدْنِي|baʿadni}} “I'm still”, {{بَعْدَك|baʿdak}} “you're still”, {{بَعْدَه|baʿda}} “he's still”, {{بَعَدْهَا|baʿadha}} “she's still”: {{بَعْدَه نَايِم|baʿda nāyim}} “he's still asleep”. **Not yet:** {{بَعَد}} + {{مَا}} + past: {{بَعَدْنِي مَا أَكَلِت|baʿadni ma akalit}} or {{مَا أَكَلِت بَعَد|ma akalit baʿad}} “I haven't eaten yet”.

blocks.means: a word that says when or for how long: just, still, yet, already.

blocks.p: **Stopped doing, not any more:** {{بَطَّل|baṭṭal}} + present: {{بَطَّل يْدَخِّن|baṭṭal ydakhkhin}} “he stopped smoking”, {{بَطَّلِت أَشْرَب گَهْوَة|baṭṭalit ashrab gahwa}} “I don't drink coffee any more”. **Until now:** {{لِحَدّ هَسَّه|li-ḥadd hassa}}.

ex.tr: I don't watch TV any more.

blocks.tip: {{بَعَد}} also means “more, else”: {{تْرِيد شِي بَعَد؟|trīd shī baʿad?}} “do you want anything else?”, and “after”: {{بَعَد الْأَكِل|baʿad il-akil}} “after the meal”.

mistakes.why: After {{بَطَّل}}, the verb is in the present.

practice.q: Your turn: say one thing you have just done, one you still do, and one you stopped doing.

answers.t: هَسَّه شْرَبِت چَاي. بَعَدْنِي أَدْرُس عَرَبِي، بَسّ بَطَّلِت أَدَخِّن.
answers.r: hassa shrabit chāy. baʿadni adrus ʿarabi, bass baṭṭalit adakhkhin.
answers.tr: I've just had tea. I'm still studying Arabic, but I've stopped smoking.

lessons.title: Join your ideas: if, because, when, who
lessons.summary: Join sentences with {{إِذَا}} and {{لَوْ}} “if”, {{لِأَنّ}} “because”, {{عَلَمُود}} “so that”, {{لَمَّن}} “when” and {{اللِّي}} “who, which”.

goal.tr: If you come tomorrow, we'll go together.

dialog.tr: Why didn't you come to the party?

dialog.t: لِأَنّ چِنِت مَرِيض. لَوْ أَدْرِي بِيهَا چَان جِيت.
dialog.r: liʾann chinit marīḍh. lō adri bīha chān jīt.
dialog.tr: Because I was ill. If I'd known about it I'd have come.
Never mind, what's past is past.

blocks.p: **If:** {{إِذَا|idha}} for what can happen, with the present or past: {{إِذَا تِتْأَخَّر، اِتَّصِل|idha titʾakhkhar, ittiṣil}} “if you're late, call”. **{{لَوْ|lō}}** for what didn't happen, with {{چَان}} in the second half: {{لَوْ أَدْرِي چَان گِلْتِلَّك|lō adri chān giltillak}} “if I'd known I'd have told you”.

blocks.means: a word that joins two parts of a sentence: and, but, if, because, when.

blocks.p: **Because:** {{لِأَنّ|liʾann}}. **So that, for:** {{عَلَمُود|ʿalamūd}} (also {{حَتَّى|ḥatta}}): {{جِيت عَلَمُود أَشُوفَك|jīt ʿalamūd ashūfak}} “I came to see you”. **When:** {{لَمَّن|lamman}}, or {{مِن|min}} for something past: {{مِن وِصَلِت، نِمِت|min wṣalit, nimit}} “when I arrived, I slept”.

**Who, which, that:** {{اللِّي|illi}} for every person and thing: {{الرِّجَّال اللِّي شِفْتَه|ir-rijjāl illi shifta}} “the man I saw”. **That** (after say, know, think): {{إِنُّو|innu}}: {{گَال إِنُّو تَعْبَان|gāl innu taʿbān}} “he said that he's tired”. **So then:** {{لَعَد|laʿad}}.

ex.tr: When you get there, call me.
This is the house I told you about.

blocks.tip: {{لَعَد|laʿad}} “so then, well then” starts a reply: {{لَعَد خَلّ نْرُوح|laʿad khall nrūḥ}} “well then, let's go”. And {{يَعْنِي|yaʿni}} “I mean” fills any pause, as in all Arabic.

mistakes.why: Spoken Arabic uses {{اللِّي}} for every “who, which”.

mistakes.tr: If I'd known, I'd have told you.

practice.tr: This is the man I saw yesterday.

options: If I'd known, I'd have come

practice.q: A colleague asks why you're leaving early.

options: لِأَنّ لَازِم آخُذ ابْنِي مِن الْمَدْرَسَة.
rs: liʾann lāzim ākhudh ibni min il-madrasa.

practice.q: Your turn: say what you'll do if it's sunny tomorrow, and why you are learning Iraqi Arabic.

answers.t: إِذَا الْجَوّ حِلُو بَاچِر، رَاح أَطْلَع. أَدْرُس عِرَاقِي لِأَنّ عِنْدِي رَبُع مِن بَغْدَاد.
answers.r: idha ij-jaww ḥilu bāchir, rāḥ aṭlaʿ. adrus ʿirāqi liʾann ʿindi rabuʿ min baghdād.
answers.tr: If the weather's nice tomorrow, I'll go out. I'm learning Iraqi because I have friends from Baghdad.
